# Trust no One, Verify Everyone: Our Zero Trust Journey


### How VTEX is rebuilding trust around identity, device, and context


[Fillipe Nunes](https://substack.com/@fillipenunes)


Sep 29, 2026


# **Trust no One, Verify Everyone: Our Zero Trust Journey**


For a long time, the security model most companies grew up with looked a lot like a nightclub with one very strict bouncer at the front door. If you got past that door, whether through the office network, a VPN, or the right login, you were “inside.” Trusted. Free to move around.


The problem is that modern work no longer has a single front door. People work from home, from airports, and from co-working spaces in other countries. Devices come and go. Services and automated systems can access company resources without a person sitting behind every request. A password that gets past the bouncer once can potentially do it again, from anywhere and at any time.


Once that became clear, the old model stopped making much sense.


At VTEX, we’ve been rebuilding that model around a simple idea: nobody gets permanent trust just because they logged in once. Every request has to earn that trust based on who or what is making it, the device involved, the context around it, and the resource being accessed.


## **What “Trust No One” actually means day to day?**


Zero Trust can sound abstract until you break it down into the questions it asks all the time, mostly in the background: is this really the person or workload we think it is? Is this a device we recognize, and is it still healthy? Does this request actually need the access it’s asking for?


Trust isn’t something you earn once and keep forever. It’s a decision that gets reassessed when the context changes.


## **Where are we on this journey?**


We’re not describing a finished project. We’re talking about work in progress across roughly 1,100 employees and close to 3,000 devices, spread across eight offices.


A few pieces are already live and improving.


We’ve started restricting where sensitive company data is allowed to go, so uploading it to the wrong destination gets caught instead of simply being assumed to be fine. Access control by itself isn’t enough. Once someone is allowed into a system, we still need to care about what happens to the data after that.


We’ve also closed a gap around security software being turned off. If a device’s protective agent stops running, whether by accident or on purpose, we now catch that far more often than we used to, and we’re pushing toward full coverage. It’s the kind of blind spot that used to show up mainly during periodic audits; now we can detect it much closer to when it actually happens.


We’re also starting to classify devices themselves, not just people, so access decisions can take into account what kind of device it is, how it’s managed, and whether its security posture meets the level of trust a specific resource requires.


**Identity is still central here, but on its own, it’s no longer enough.**


That same principle is now extending into the browser, since for many employees that’s where most of the actual work happens. We’re starting to manage that environment more explicitly and keep corporate work tied to the corporate identity.


That gives us a clearer boundary between personal and company contexts and lets us apply security policies closer to where access actually takes place, not just at the device or network level. It’s another version of the same principle: identity matters, but the context around that identity matters too.


## **Why We’re Doing This the Hard Way**


In the short term, it would be easier to keep trusting the front door. Zero Trust means more friction to design around, more systems that need to exchange signals, and more decisions that have to happen dynamically instead of relying on a one-time login.


We’re making that trade anyway because trusting a perimeter that barely exists anymore isn’t actually safer. It’s just more familiar.


**A stolen password shouldn’t be a skeleton key.** A compromised laptop shouldn’t get the same trust as a healthy one just because it already has access. And an automated process acting on someone’s behalf shouldn’t inherit unlimited trust simply because it holds valid credentials.


That’s the real shift underneath all of this: moving away from “is this user inside or outside?” and toward “does this request still make sense, from this identity, on this device, under these conditions, for this resource?”


It’s slower and less glamorous than catching a dramatic breach in progress. But it’s also the kind of work that prevents many of those moments from happening in the first place.


We’re still building this, piece by piece, quarter by quarter. But the direction is set: access isn’t a door you walk through once. It’s a question we keep asking every step.
